topic: Hindsight bias: 'I knew it all along'
title: 'I Knew It All Along': The Hindsight Trap
voiceover: Do you ever say, 'I knew it all along'? Knowing the outcome made people judge it as more likely. That's from 1975, when Baruch Fischhoff studied what happens when people learn an outcome. People were largely unaware of this effect. So they overestimated what they would have known without the outcome. They also overestimated what others actually knew beforehand. In 2012, Neal Roese and Kathleen Vohs reviewed the research. Roese and Vohs say it is the first overview to draw on research across disciplines. They proposed three levels of hindsight bias, from memory distortion to higher-level belief. The first is misremembering what you predicted. So when you feel 'I knew it', check whether you wrote down what you actually predicted. Tomorrow: what does multitasking really cost you?

description: Do you really know it all along? Fischhoff's 1975 experiments showed that learning an outcome makes it seem more likely, and people overestimate what they knew beforehand. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Fischhoff, B. (1975). Hindsight is not equal to foresight: The effect of outcome knowledge on judgment under uncertainty. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, 1(3), 288-299. Source: Roese, N. J., & Vohs, K. D. (2012). Hindsight bias. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 7(5), 411-426.
accuracy_note: Fischhoff's 1975 findings are from lab judgment tasks; Roese & Vohs (2012) review the broader literature and propose three levels of hindsight bias. The video's takeaway about checking written predictions is an application of the memory-distortion level, not a tested intervention.
